newsitem.title: USA: U.S. NRC gets mixed reviews on tougher enforcement.
newsitem.headline: U.S. NRC gets mixed reviews on tougher enforcement.

text.p: Moves Wednesday by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission to clamp down on unsafe nuclear power plants over the last year drew more questions than praise about the agency's vigilance over the industry.
NRC commissioners and critics of the agency alike hailed the increased scrutiny of bad plants, but questioned why the agency had not acted sooner.
The commission announced that it had added five nuclear power stations, for a total of eight, to its watchlist of problem plants, which is updated twice a year.

One of the five that were added, the Salem 1 unit owned by Public Service Electric and Gas, was targeted last year by consumer advocacy group Public Citizen as the worst nuclear reactor in the United States.
NRC senior managers Wednesday put Salem 1, which first had problems in 1990, on the watchlist retroactively.

"A decision was made to recognize that Salem should have been placed on the watchlist previously and that it would not have been removed if it had been," said Hub Miller, NRC administrator for the Northeast region.
Similarly, the NRC put the troubled Maine Yankee plant, owned by Northeast Utilities, on the watchlist.
NRC Chairwoman Shirley Jackson said the addition of Maine Yankee, which had been considered a "good performer," suggested that the NRC had failed to uncover problems earlier.
"What assurances do we have that we're not missing them somewhere else?" Jackson asked NRC senior managers.
"Early ... guidance from the NRC is needed to avoid the situations that have led to this point," said Commissioner Nis Diaz, commenting on the larger number of plants on the list.

David Lochbaum, nuclear safety engineer at the Union of Concerned Scientists, said the commission should take steps to prevent problems, rather than becoming more vigilant after several violations have been reported at a plant.
Nevertheless, Lochbaum and the Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI), which represents nuclear utilities, said most utilities are aggressively meeting safety and performance regulations.
Risky incidents, or "significant safety events", per plant have fallen from 2.4 per plant in 1985 to 0.1 in 1995, NEI spokesman Steve Unglesbee said.
Lochbaum said the NRC had effectively allowed the bad plants to operate more cheaply than their competitors.
"Plants that are not meeting the regulations are being given an unfair cost advantage," he said.
But Rep. Ed Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat who has pressed for more rigorous nuclear regulation, said the NRC was moving in the right direction.

"The NRC has to ensure that they be a watchdog and not a lapdog for the nuclear industry," Markey said. "My hope is that they now institute a much more rigorous safety-minded set of standards," he said in a telephone interview.
Markey last year asked the General Accounting Office, the Congressional watchdog, to review the listing process and the progress of listed plants. The report is expected next fall.

Critics of the agency hailed its warning that Commonwealth Edison, the nation's largest nuclear utility, must justify why six of its nuclear units at three power stations should be allowed to operate.

"The NRC is really sending a very strong warning to the operators of Commonwealth Edison," said Public Citizen's critical mass energy project director Bill Magavern. "It's showing much more life than it has in years."

Senior NRC managers said Wednesday they had not yet adopted recommendations by management consultants Arthur Andersen for improving the process. Those recommendations are to be discussed at a future meeting.
"We want to see NRC move toward an appraisal process that focuses only on objective measures," NEI's Unglesbee said.
